Fibrous tunic.description: The sclera is the tough white outer wall of the eyeball, made of dense irregular connective tissue rich in type I collagen. The cornea at the front is the clear, avascular window that provides most of the eye's refracting power. At the corneoscleral edge, the trabecular meshwork drains aqueous humour into the canal of Schlemm.
clinical: Glaucoma

Raised pressure inside the eye, usually from reduced outflow of aqueous humour through the trabecular meshwork, can damage the optic nerve. Open-angle glaucoma often causes slow loss of peripheral vision without pain.
Corneal scarring
Infection, injury or dystrophy can leave the cornea cloudy and blur vision. A corneal transplant (keratoplasty) can restore clarity when scarring is severe.

Vascular tunic (uvea).description: The uvea is the pigmented, blood-rich middle layer of the eyeball. The choroid at the back nourishes the outer retina. The ciliary body makes aqueous humour, and its ciliary muscle changes the shape of the lens for focusing, while the iris changes pupil size to control how much light enters.
clinical: Uveitis
Inflammation of the uvea causes eye pain, redness and light sensitivity, and needs prompt treatment to protect vision.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
The peripheral iris can bow forward and block the drainage angle, causing a sudden rise in eye pressure with severe pain, headache, nausea and a red eye. It is an emergency.

Nervous tunic (retina).description: The retina is the light-sensitive inner layer lining the back of the eye. Rods and cones convert light into nerve signals that pass through bipolar and ganglion cells, whose axons leave the eye as the optic nerve. The macula and fovea give sharp central vision, and the optic disc, where the nerve leaves, has no photoreceptors and forms the blind spot.
clinical: Retinal detachment
The neural retina can separate from the pigment layer beneath it, causing flashes, floaters and a curtain-like shadow over vision. It is an emergency needing urgent treatment.
Age-related macular degeneration
Degeneration of the macula, mostly in people over 50, damages the central vision needed for reading and recognising faces, while peripheral vision is usually preserved.

Lens & zonule.description: The lens is a transparent, flexible, biconvex body behind the iris that focuses light onto the retina. Zonular fibres hold it in place around the ciliary body; when the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonules slacken and the lens becomes rounder for near vision.
clinical: Cataract
Clouding of the lens causes gradual, painless blurring and glare. Surgery replacing the cloudy lens with an artificial one is one of the most common operations worldwide.
Lens displacement in Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome, caused by fibrillin-1 defects, weakens the zonular fibres so the lens can shift, most often upwards (ectopia lentis).

Anterior segment (aqueous humor).description: Aqueous humour is a clear watery fluid made by the ciliary processes. It fills the anterior chamber in front of the iris and the posterior chamber behind it, nourishes the avascular cornea and lens, and leaves the eye mainly through the trabecular meshwork.
clinical: Hypopyon
Pus collecting in the anterior chamber, seen in severe eye infection or inflammation, forms a visible level at the bottom of the chamber.
Blocked aqueous drainage
Aqueous humour is made continuously by the ciliary processes; if its outflow is blocked, pressure rises and glaucoma can result.

Posterior segment (vitreous chamber).description: The vitreous body is a clear, gel-like mass, about 4 mL, that fills the large space behind the lens. It is mostly water held in a fine collagen and hyaluronan network, and it helps keep the retina flat against the back of the eye.
clinical: Posterior vitreous detachment
With age the vitreous liquefies and can pull away from the retina, causing new floaters and flashes of light. It is usually harmless, but occasionally it tears the retina, which needs checking.
Optic neuritis
Inflammation of the optic nerve causes pain on eye movement and blurred or dimmed vision, often in one eye. It can be an early sign of multiple sclerosis.
Central retinal artery occlusion
A blocked central retinal artery causes sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye; the retina often looks pale, with a cherry-red spot at the macula. It is an emergency.

Extrinsic eye muscles.description: Six extraocular muscles move each eyeball: four rectus muscles and two oblique muscles, all supplied by cranial nerves III, IV and VI. The recti arise from the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit, and the superior oblique tendon passes through the trochlea, a pulley on the orbit's upper inner wall. Also included is the levator palpebrae superioris, which lifts the upper eyelid.
clinical: Cranial nerve palsy
Damage to cranial nerve III, IV or VI weakens the muscles it supplies, causing double vision. For example, a sixth-nerve palsy stops the lateral rectus turning the eye outward.
Strabismus
Misalignment of the eyes, which can result from imbalance between these muscles, stops the two eyes fixing on the same point and can lead to amblyopia if untreated in childhood.
Ptosis
Drooping of the upper eyelid, from weakness of levator palpebrae superioris or damage to cranial nerve III, can partly block vision.
Chalazion
A blocked meibomian gland forms a painless lump in the eyelid, called a chalazion.

Conjunctiva.description: The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that lines the inside of the eyelids and folds back over the white of the eye, forming recesses called fornices. Goblet cells in it make mucus for the tear film, and it ends at the limbus, where the clear cornea begins.
clinical: Conjunctivitis
Inflammation of the conjunctiva makes the eye red and sticky or watery. Most cases are viral or allergic and settle on their own, though bacterial infection may need antibiotic drops.
Pterygium
A wedge-shaped fold of fibrovascular tissue growing from the bulbar conjunctiva can spread onto the cornea, usually from the nasal side, and is linked to long-term sun exposure.

Lacrimal apparatus.description: The lacrimal gland, in the upper outer part of the orbit, makes the watery layer of tears. Tears spread across the eye with each blink and drain through the puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct into the nose.
clinical: Dry eye
Reduced or poor-quality tears leave the eye dry, gritty and irritated. Causes include ageing, some medicines and autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome, which also damages the lacrimal gland.
Blocked tear drainage
A blocked nasolacrimal duct causes watering of the eye and can lead to infection of the lacrimal sac. Blockage is common in newborns and often clears within the first year.

parts.description: The sclera is the tough, opaque white outer wall of the eyeball, forming the posterior five-sixths of the fibrous tunic. It is made of dense irregular connective tissue rich in type I collagen, and the extraocular muscles attach to its outer surface. Behind the eye it is pierced by the optic nerve, and the choroid lies against its inner face.

The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped front window of the eye, continuous with the sclera at the limbus. It has five layers from the front: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, Bowman's layer, the stroma, Descemet's membrane and a single layer of endothelium. It is transparent and avascular, nourished by tears and aqueous humour, and it provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power.

The limbus is the narrow transition zone where the transparent cornea meets the opaque sclera, also called the corneoscleral junction. Its basal epithelium holds the limbal stem cells, which sit in the palisades of Vogt (radial ridges of epithelium) and renew the corneal epithelium. Just behind it, the trabecular meshwork and scleral venous sinus lie in the angle of the anterior chamber. If these stem cells are lost, conjunctival cells can grow across the cornea and cloud it.

The trabecular meshwork is a sponge-like filter of collagen beams covered by trabecular cells, lying in the iridocorneal angle where the cornea meets the iris. It drains aqueous humour from the anterior chamber into the canal of Schlemm, which lies just outside it. Resistance to this outflow sets the intraocular pressure, and raised resistance here underlies primary open-angle glaucoma.

The scleral venous sinus, or canal of Schlemm, is a ring-shaped channel that runs around the anterior chamber angle, just inside the sclera. Its thin wall is lined by endothelial cells and has no smooth muscle. It collects aqueous humour from the trabecular meshwork and passes it through small collector channels into the episcleral veins.

The choroid is the thin, dark, blood-rich layer of the uvea lying between the retina and the sclera. It is made mostly of blood vessels and melanocytes, and its capillary layer (the choriocapillaris) nourishes the outer retina, including the photoreceptors. Its pigment absorbs stray light, and in the living eye it can give the fundus a tessellated, mottled appearance.

The ciliary body is the ring-shaped thickening of uveal tissue that joins the iris to the choroid. It contains the ciliary muscle, which changes lens shape, and the ciliary processes, whose double epithelium secretes aqueous humour. Zonular fibres run from the ciliary processes to the lens capsule, holding the lens in place. In a section it appears as a triangular wedge with folded processes on its inner surface.

The ciliary muscle is a ring of smooth muscle inside the ciliary body, attached to the sclera at the scleral spur. Its meridional, radial and circular fibres pull on the zonular fibres, so that when it contracts the zonules slacken and the lens becomes rounder for near vision. It is supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve (CN III), which relay through the ciliary ganglion.

The ciliary processes are a ring of radial folds on the inner surface of the ciliary body, forming the ciliary crown seen through a dilated pupil. Each fold has a core of blood vessels covered by two epithelial layers, and the inner non-pigmented layer secretes aqueous humour. Zonular fibres attach to them, so they help support the lens.

The iris is the coloured, circular diaphragm lying between the cornea and the lens, with the pupil at its centre. Its stroma contains melanocytes whose pigment gives the eye its colour, and the sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles lie within it and change the pupil's size. Its outer edge is continuous with the ciliary body, and its back surface is the iris pigment epithelium.

The sphincter pupillae is a ring of smooth muscle in the iris stroma, lying close to the pupil's free edge. It constricts the pupil in bright light, and it is supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). In a section it appears as a band of spindle-shaped muscle cells encircling the pupil.

The dilator pupillae is a thin sheet of myoepithelial cells arranged radially in the posterior part of the iris stroma, next to the pigment epithelium. It enlarges the pupil in dim light, and it is supplied by sympathetic fibres. Loss of this sympathetic supply, as in Horner syndrome, leaves the pupil small and constricted.

The iris pigment epithelium is the double layer of densely pigmented cells that forms the back surface of the iris. It is continuous with the pigmented epithelium of the ciliary body and the retina, and its pigment stops light passing through the iris. In a section it appears as a dark band behind the stroma.

The pupil is the round central opening of the iris, through which light passes to reach the lens and retina. It is an aperture rather than a tissue, and its size is set by the sphincter and dilator pupillae, constricting in bright light and dilating in dim light. It looks black because little light is reflected back from the eye's dark interior.

The pigmented layer of the retina, or retinal pigment epithelium, is a single layer of cuboidal, melanin-containing cells lying between the neural retina and Bruch's membrane. It absorbs stray light and engulfs the tips of the photoreceptor outer segments each day, recycling them. It transports nutrients, recycles vitamin A for the visual cycle, and forms the outer blood-retina barrier. In a section, it is the dark cell layer at the outer margin of the retina.

The neural layer of the retina is the inner, light-sensitive part of the retina, containing the rods and cones together with bipolar, ganglion, horizontal and amacrine cells. It lies inside the pigmented layer, so light passes through its inner layers before reaching the photoreceptors. In a section its layers appear as rows of nuclei separated by synaptic (plexiform) zones. Its separation from the pigmented layer is a retinal detachment.

The ora serrata is the wavy, toothed front edge of the neural retina, where the retina meets the ciliary body. Beyond it, the pigmented and non-pigmented epithelia continue forward over the ciliary body and iris without any light-sensitive cells. Viewed through a dilated pupil it looks scalloped, and the strong vitreous attachment here makes it a common site for retinal tears.

The macula lutea is the yellowish, central area of the retina around the fovea, coloured by the yellow pigments lutein and zeaxanthin. It has a high density of cones and provides detailed central vision. On the fundus it appears as a slightly darker patch temporal to the optic disc, and age-related macular degeneration damages this area.

The fovea centralis is a shallow pit at the centre of the macula where the inner retinal layers are pushed aside, so light reaches the cones directly. It contains only cones, with no rods, and it gives the sharpest vision. In central retinal artery occlusion, the surrounding retina turns pale while the fovea looks cherry red, because the choroid shows through its thin centre.

The optic disc is the round, pale area on the nasal side of the fundus where ganglion cell axons converge and leave the eye as the optic nerve. It contains no photoreceptors, so it forms the physiological blind spot, and the central retinal artery and vein enter and leave here. On ophthalmoscopy it appears as a paler circle with a central cup, and swelling (papilloedema) or cupping in glaucoma can be seen.

The lens capsule is a smooth, transparent, elastic basement membrane that completely encloses the lens. It is made of type IV collagen and laid down by the lens epithelium, which lies beneath its front surface. Zonular fibres attach to it around the equator, and a capsulorhexis is cut in it during cataract surgery. In a section it appears as a sharp, eosinophilic line around the lens.

The zonular fibres, or suspensory ligament of the lens, are fine fibrils made of fibrillin-rich microfibrils that form a ring from the ciliary processes to the lens capsule. They hold the lens in position and transmit the forces that change its shape. When the ciliary muscle contracts, the fibres slacken and the lens becomes rounder for near vision.

The anterior chamber is the fluid-filled space between the back of the cornea and the front of the iris. It is filled with aqueous humour, which enters from the posterior chamber through the pupil. Aqueous humour leaves through the iridocorneal angle at the trabecular meshwork, and when the iris blocks this angle, angle-closure glaucoma can result.

The posterior chamber is the narrow space between the back of the iris and the front of the lens, bounded at its edge by the ciliary processes and zonular fibres. Aqueous humour is secreted into it by the ciliary processes, and it then flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber. In life it is very narrow, with the iris lying close to the lens.

The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) is made of about 1.2 million axons of retinal ganglion cells that run from the optic disc to the optic chiasm. The axons become myelinated by oligodendrocytes just behind the lamina cribrosa, which makes the nerve widen behind the eye. Although it is a central nervous system tract, it is wrapped in the three meninges and cannot regenerate. Inflammation of it, as in optic neuritis from multiple sclerosis, causes painful loss of vision.

The dural sheath of the optic nerve is the outer meningeal covering of the nerve, continuous with the dura mater of the brain and fused with the sclera at the front of the eye. Inside it lie the arachnoid and pia mater, and the subarachnoid space here is continuous with that around the brain. Raised intracranial pressure transmitted along this space can compress the nerve and central retinal vein, causing papilloedema (swelling of the optic disc).

The central retinal artery is the first branch of the ophthalmic artery, which arises from the internal carotid. It runs inside the optic nerve, about 1 cm behind the eyeball, and reaches the optic disc, where it divides to supply the inner layers of the retina. Its branches are end arteries, so blockage causes sudden painless loss of vision with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. On fundoscopy its arterioles look narrower and brighter than the accompanying veins.

The central retinal vein drains the retina and runs through the centre of the optic nerve beside the central retinal artery, leaving the eye at the optic disc. Behind the eye it crosses the subarachnoid space and drains into the superior ophthalmic vein or the cavernous sinus. Across the fundus its tributaries run alongside the arteries, appearing darker and wider on ophthalmoscopy. Occlusion of the vein causes widespread retinal haemorrhages, giving a 'stormy sunset' fundus.

The superior rectus is one of the four straight extraocular muscles that move the eyeball. It arises from the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit, runs forward along the roof of the orbit, and inserts into the upper front of the sclera. It mainly elevates the eye, and it also turns the eye inwards and rolls the top of the cornea towards the nose. It is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Inferior rectus: one of the four rectus muscles that move the eyeball. It arises from the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit, runs forward along the orbital floor and inserts on the lower surface of the eyeball near its front. It depresses the eye (looks down), turns it inwards and rotates the top of the eye outwards. It is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Medial rectus: one of the four rectus muscles, arising from the common tendinous ring at the back of the orbit. It runs forward along the inner wall of the orbit and inserts on the inner side of the eyeball. Its main action is to turn the eye inwards, towards the nose (adduction). It is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Lateral rectus: a rectus muscle that arises from the common tendinous ring by two heads and runs along the outer wall of the orbit to insert on the outer side of the eyeball. Its job is to turn the eye outwards, away from the nose (abduction). It is the only extraocular muscle supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI), so a palsy of that nerve leaves the eye unable to turn outwards and it tends to turn inwards (squint).

Superior oblique: a slender extraocular muscle that starts at the body of the sphenoid, above and medial to the optic canal, not from the common tendinous ring. Its tendon passes through the trochlea, a cartilaginous pulley at the upper inner corner of the orbit, then bends back to attach to the upper, outer back of the eyeball. It mainly turns the top of the eye inwards (intorsion), and also depresses and abducts the eye. It is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV).

Trochlea: a small pulley of cartilage fixed to a shallow pit, the trochlear fossa, on the frontal bone at the upper inner corner of the orbit. The tendon of the superior oblique muscle runs through this loop and changes direction before reaching the eyeball. The trochlea is a pulley, not a muscle, and it lets the superior oblique pull the eye downwards and outwards.

Inferior oblique: the only extraocular muscle that does not arise from the back of the orbit. It starts from the orbital floor near the nasolacrimal groove, runs backwards and outwards beneath the eyeball and inserts on its outer, back surface. It raises the eye and turns it outwards, and it also extorts the eye, rotating the top of the cornea outwards. It is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn): a fibrous ring at the back of the orbit, around the optic canal and the inner part of the superior orbital fissure, from which the four rectus muscles arise. The optic nerve and ophthalmic artery pass through the optic canal inside the ring, while the oculomotor, abducens and nasociliary nerves pass through the ring into the muscle cone, the space behind the eyeball enclosed by the rectus muscles. Lesions at this orbital apex can damage several of these nerves at once.

Upper eyelid (superior palpebra): the mobile fold of skin and muscle that covers the front of the eyeball and is raised by the levator palpebrae superioris. It spreads the tear film with each blink and shuts out light during sleep. From front to back, its main layers are skin, loose areolar tissue, orbicularis oculi, the orbital septum, the tarsal plate with its meibomian glands, and the palpebral conjunctiva. The lid meets the lower lid at the medial and lateral canthi, and the gap between them is the palpebral fissure.

Lower eyelid (inferior palpebra): a smaller, less mobile fold than the upper lid, with the same main layers: skin, loose areolar tissue, orbicularis oculi, the orbital septum, a narrow tarsal plate with meibomian glands, and palpebral conjunctiva. It is drawn down by the capsulopalpebral fascia, an extension of the inferior rectus sheath, as the eye looks downwards. Its margin carries the lower lashes and, at its inner end, the lower lacrimal punctum. With age it may sag outwards (ectropion) or turn inwards (entropion).

Superior tarsal plate (upper tarsus): a crescent-shaped plate of dense fibrous connective tissue, about 10 mm high, that gives the upper eyelid its shape and stiffness. The meibomian glands lie embedded in it, the levator aponeurosis attaches to its front, and the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments anchor its ends to the orbital margins. To look for a foreign body under the upper lid, the lid is turned inside out over a cotton bud so the tarsal plate can be examined.

Inferior tarsal plate (lower tarsus): a smaller plate of dense fibrous tissue, about 4-5 mm high, in the lower eyelid. It holds the lower meibomian glands and is anchored at its ends by the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments, with the capsulopalpebral fascia attached along its lower border. Laxity of these supports, common with age, lets the lower lid turn outwards (ectropion) or inwards (entropion).

Tarsal (meibomian) glands: long, vertical sebaceous glands embedded in the tarsal plates of both lids, each with a central duct from which cell-filled acini bud off. Their ducts open in a row on the lid margin just behind the eyelashes, and their oily secretion, meibum, forms the outer lipid layer of the tear film, slowing evaporation. Blockage can cause evaporative dry eye and a painless, firm lump called a chalazion; an infected gland is an internal hordeolum (stye).

Orbicularis oculi (palpebral part): a thin, pale sheet of skeletal muscle lying in front of the tarsal plates, arising from the medial palpebral ligament and inserting into the lateral palpebral raphe. It closes the lids gently during blinking and sleep. Its lacrimal part, behind the lacrimal sac, helps pump tears into the sac with each blink. It is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII); in Bell palsy the eye cannot close and the cornea can dry.

Superior tarsal muscle (Müller muscle): a thin sheet of smooth muscle running from the underside of the levator palpebrae superioris to the upper border of the superior tarsal plate. It is supplied by sympathetic nerves and raises the upper lid by about 1-2 mm. Loss of its tone in Horner syndrome causes a mild drooping of the lid, together with a small pupil, while overactivity of the muscle contributes to upper lid retraction in thyroid eye disease.

Eyelashes (cilia): short, thick, curved hairs set in two or three rows along the front edge of each lid margin, curving away from the eye. Touching them triggers a blink, and they help keep dust and particles out of the eye. Each follicle has sebaceous glands (of Zeis) and apocrine sweat glands (of Moll), and an infected follicle is an external stye (hordeolum). Lashes that turn inwards (trichiasis), as in trachoma, rub and scar the cornea.

Medial canthus (medial palpebral commissure): the angle at the inner corner of the eye where the upper and lower eyelids meet. It holds the lacrimal lake, a small pool of tears, with the pink lacrimal caruncle and the plica semilunaris beside it, and the lacrimal puncta open on the lid margins here. The medial palpebral ligament anchors the lids to the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla, so this corner stays fixed as the lids move.

Lateral canthus (lateral palpebral commissure): the outer angle where the upper and lower eyelids meet, usually lying slightly higher than the inner corner. The lateral palpebral raphe, a fibrous band where the orbicularis oculi inserts, lies here, and the lateral palpebral ligament (lateral canthal tendon) anchors the lids to the orbital tubercle on the zygomatic bone. Laxity of this tendon lets the lower lid sag outwards (ectropion).

Palpebral conjunctiva: the thin, transparent mucous membrane that lines the inner surface of each eyelid, bound firmly to the tarsal plate beneath so that it moves with the lid. It turns back at the fornices to become the bulbar conjunctiva over the eyeball. Goblet cells in its epithelium secrete mucus for the tear film, and its fine blood vessels make it look pink, reddening in conjunctivitis.

Superior conjunctival fornix: the deep, curved recess where the conjunctiva of the upper eyelid turns back onto the eyeball, forming the upper boundary of the conjunctival sac. It is deeper than the lower fornix, and the excretory ducts of the lacrimal gland open into its outer part. Grit tends to lodge in this recess, so the upper lid is everted to search for foreign bodies.

Inferior conjunctival fornix: the shallower recess at the lower edge of the conjunctival sac, where the conjunctiva of the lower eyelid turns back onto the eyeball. It is the usual pocket for instilling eye drops, which are placed by gently pulling the lower lid down to form it.

Bulbar conjunctiva: the thin, transparent part of the conjunctiva that covers the front of the white of the eye (sclera), from the fornices to the limbus. It is loosely attached to the sclera, so it slides freely over the eyeball as the eye moves, and it ends at the limbus where the clear cornea begins. Its goblet cells supply mucus for the tear film, and a yellowish, degenerative patch on it near the limbus is a pinguecula.

Lacrimal caruncle: a small, pinkish, fleshy mound in the medial canthus, medial to the plica semilunaris and at the edge of the lacrimal lake. Despite its name it is not part of the drainage system; it is a modified patch of skin with fine hairs, sebaceous glands and sweat glands, covered by stratified squamous epithelium. It stands out as a skin-like bump at the inner corner, unlike the smooth conjunctiva around it.

Plica semilunaris: a small, vertical, crescent-shaped fold of bulbar conjunctiva in the medial canthus, lateral to the caruncle. It is a vestigial remnant of the nictitating membrane, the third eyelid that birds and many other animals use to sweep across the eye. Its folded conjunctiva stretches as the eye turns, and it contains goblet cells that help keep the medial corner moist.

Levator palpebrae superioris: the muscle that raises the upper eyelid. It arises from the underside of the lesser wing of the sphenoid, above the optic canal, runs forward over the roof of the orbit and ends in a broad aponeurosis that inserts into the front of the upper tarsal plate and the skin of the lid. It is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III), so a CN III palsy droops the lid (ptosis).

Excretory ducts of lacrimal gland: several small ducts that carry tears from the gland to the surface of the eye. The gland has a large orbital lobe in the upper outer orbit and a smaller palpebral lobe in the upper lid, and these ducts drain both parts. They open into the outer part of the upper conjunctival fornix, where tiny openings can be seen when the upper lid is turned over.

Lacrimal puncta: the two tiny openings, one on each eyelid, at the inner end of the lid margin. They sit on small raised lacrimal papillae at the edge of the lacrimal lake and take in tears to start the drainage pathway through the canaliculi. A blocked punctum makes the eye overflow with tears (epiphora), because the tears cannot drain away.

Lacrimal canaliculi: two narrow channels, an upper and a lower, that connect each lacrimal punctum to the lacrimal sac. Each begins as a short vertical channel at the lid margin, then turns medially for about 1 cm, often joining its partner to form a common canaliculus before entering the sac. Their lining is stratified squamous epithelium.

Lacrimal sac: the expanded upper end of the nasolacrimal drainage passage, lying in the lacrimal fossa beside the nose, a groove formed by the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla. Tears from the canaliculi collect here and pass down into the nasolacrimal duct, and the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi helps pump them in with each blink. Infection of the sac (dacryocystitis) causes a painful, red swelling at the inner corner of the eye, beside the nose.

Nasolacrimal duct: the passage that continues downwards from the lacrimal sac through a bony canal in the maxilla and lacrimal bone, and opens into the front of the inferior meatus beneath the inferior nasal concha. It carries tears from the eye into the nose, which is why crying makes the nose run. Its lower opening is partly guarded by a mucosal fold, the valve of Hasner, which is a common site of blockage in newborns.
